1387.title: The dark night, again
1387.hook: John of the Cross: God works in darkness, weaning us from feelings
1387.howItsDone: Catholics honor John of the Cross as a saint and Doctor of the Church, and his poem and commentary are read by Christians of several churches; spiritual directors draw on his advice to help people tell a season of dryness in prayer apart from depression or neglect.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Mother Teresa's letters, and a saint who kept going without feeling God near. Your line was faith without feeling.

A tiny cell. Almost no light. Tradition says a Spanish friar named John was locked in a room like this by members of his own religious order, who didn't like his reforms. No books. Bread and water. And in that darkness, tradition says, he began to compose poems in his head. Out of that time, the story goes, came a poem that begins on a dark night, a soul slipping out of a quiet house, unseen, guided by no light except the one burning in the heart. We met this phrase in year one. Today, a sharper question: what is the darkness for?

John later wrote a long explanation of his poem, and at its center is a mother and a child. At first, he says, God treats a new believer like a mother nursing a baby: warm, sweet, easy. Prayer feels good. Then, like any mother, God begins to wean the child. The sweetness is taken away, not to punish, but so the child can grow up and eat real food. The Psalms already use the image: "my soul is even as a weaned child." And Paul tells the Corinthians, "I have fed you with milk, and not with meat." Why wean at all? John says a soul can come to love the good feelings of prayer more than God. So God gently removes the feelings. What's left, in his telling, if you stay, is a love that doesn't depend on getting something back. John was careful, too. Not every dryness is this night, he wrote; some comes from sin, carelessness or sickness of body and mind, and he told guides to tell them apart. Hold that next to a lesson from a few days ago: depression needs care and help, and naming something a dark night is no reason to skip it. And inside the night? John's advice is simple: don't strain to force the old feelings back. Stay quiet, with a loving attention, and let God work. The psalm says, "the darkness and the light are both alike to thee." In the psalm, the night isn't empty to God.

Close your eyes and let the darkness behind your eyelids be just what it is, with no special feeling, picture or answer to chase. Stay with a quiet, open attention, the way you'd sit in a dark room waiting for your eyes to adjust. If you pray, rest there before God without words; if you don't, rest in the not-knowing.
The dark night. John of the Cross's name for the season when God takes away prayer's sweetness, as a mother weans a child, so love can grow.
Your line: night is working. For John, even the dark was going somewhere. See you tomorrow.

1388.title: The silence of God
1388.hook: Psalm 22 and the cross both hold God's silence
1388.howItsDone: Some churches read Psalm 22 in Holy Week, and on Holy Saturday some churches strip the altar, silence the bells and hold no ordinary service until the Easter Vigil, keeping the day as one of waiting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the dark night: John of the Cross and a mother weaning her child from the sweetness. Your line was night is working.

"O my God, I cry in the day time, but thou hearest not; and in the night season, and am not silent." That's the second verse of Psalm twenty-two, a song addressed to the chief musician, set down by someone who has called out day and night and heard nothing back. Some people live that line long before they find it in the Bible: the phone that doesn't ring, the prayer that seems to hit the ceiling. And this is the psalm Jesus reaches for on the cross.

Year two had a psalm about waiting in silence. This silence is harder. The psalm names it honestly. It doesn't pretend God answered: thou hearest not. And that line was kept in the Psalms, to be prayed instead of hidden. Then the cross. Matthew records Jesus crying out, "Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" Those are the opening words of this same psalm. At his baptism, Matthew says, a voice spoke from heaven. Here, the Gospel records no voice in reply. Only the cry, and soon after, his death. Christians have read this moment in different ways: some hear Jesus truly feeling abandoned; others note he's praying a psalm that turns to trust. Some hold both. And the psalm does turn. Further on it says God "hath not despised nor abhorred the affliction of the afflicted; neither hath he hid his face from him; but when he cried unto him, he heard." The psalm that began with thou hearest not comes round to he heard. For the psalmist, silence wasn't the same as absence. Last, a day of silence on the calendar. Between Good Friday and Easter morning comes Holy Saturday. In some churches the altar is stripped bare and the bells stay quiet. Nothing is announced. The body lies in the tomb. Lamentations has a line for days like that: "It is good that a man should both hope and quietly wait for the salvation of the LORD." The churches that mark it keep that waiting on purpose.

Let the room go quiet, with no music, no words, no list, and if a question has been sitting in you without an answer, let it be there, unanswered. Notice that silence has a texture: a hum, a breath, a car far away. If you pray, wait before God without saying anything at all; if you don't, wait anyway, and let the quiet be enough.
The silence of God. The stretch when prayer seems to meet nothing, prayed in Psalm twenty-two and on the cross, and kept each year on Holy Saturday.
Your line: silence is not absence. Holy Saturday still comes before Easter morning. Until tomorrow.

1389.title: Unanswered prayer (2 Corinthians 12:7–9)
1389.hook: Paul asked three times for a thorn to be removed, and it wasn't
1389.howItsDone: Christians keep praying for healing and help for themselves and others, and when an answer doesn't come, some turn to Paul's thorn and Jesus's prayer in Gethsemane, praying for grace to carry what remains.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the silence of God: Psalm twenty-two begins thou hearest not and turns to he heard. Your line was silence is not absence.

Paul, writing to the church in Corinth, admits he has something wrong with him. He doesn't say what. He calls it a thorn in the flesh. And he prayed for it to go: "For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me." Thrice. Three times he asked, and three times, as far as we can tell, the thorn stayed exactly where it was. The apostle writing this letter had a prayer that didn't get the answer he asked for.

Paul calls it "a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me," and he never names it. Some readers guess an illness, or trouble with his eyes. Others think it was a person, an opponent who kept dogging his work. Others think it was a temptation. Because Paul leaves it unnamed, some readers set their own thorn in that space. Then the answer. It's not silence, and it's not yes: "And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness." The thorn stays. What's promised instead is grace, enough of it, for living with the thing that didn't go away. Some Christians say every prayer gets an answer, and sometimes the answer is no. Paul's story has a second half: no, and here is what will carry you. He isn't the only one who asked three times. In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus prays, "O my Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me: nevertheless not as I will, but as thou wilt." Matthew says he goes back and prays a third time, saying the same words. And the cup doesn't pass. Paul's thorn and Jesus's cup sit side by side: real requests, honestly made, and a road that went on anyway. Notice, too, that Paul didn't stop after the first time. Three tries before he heard the answer. Unanswered prayer, in this text, isn't prayer that failed. It's prayer that was heard, and answered with something other than what was asked.

Name one thing that's stayed with you however much you've wanted it gone: a health problem, a hard relationship, a habit, a loss. Don't try to solve it. If you pray, ask God about it once more, honestly, the way Paul did, and listen for what might carry you if it stays; if you don't, hold it, and ask what has helped you live with it so far.
Unanswered prayer. A prayer that seems to get no, like Paul's thrice-asked thorn, answered instead with grace that is enough.
Your line: my grace is sufficient. The thorn stayed, and so did the grace. Same time tomorrow.

1390.title: Strength in weakness (2 Corinthians 12:10)
1390.hook: when I am weak, then I am strong
1390.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to 2 Corinthians 12 in illness, addiction recovery and hard seasons, and some churches and recovery groups speak openly about weakness and dependence on God and on one another rather than hiding them.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Paul asked three times for the thorn to go. Your line was my grace is sufficient.

Paul had critics in Corinth, and he quotes them in his own letter. His letters, they say, are "weighty and powerful; but his bodily presence is weak, and his speech contemptible." Strong on paper, unimpressive in person. The obvious reply to a review like that is a list of achievements. Paul starts one, then turns it upside down. Instead of hiding his weak points, he puts them on display: the beatings, the shipwrecks, the sleepless nights, the thorn. Then he writes a line that turns it all around.
screen: `HE PUTS HIS WEAK POINTS ON DISPLAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the line, right after the thorn: "Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ's sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong." Notice the word therefore. It follows from yesterday's answer, my strength is made perfect in weakness. Paul isn't saying weakness is good in itself. It's the place where a strength not his own shows up. Just before: "Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me." Earlier in the same letter there's a picture: "But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellency of the power may be of God, and not of us." Clay jars. Cheap, breakable kitchen pottery, holding treasure. If the jar were gold, you'd admire the jar. Because it's clay, you notice what's inside. This isn't only Paul's private mood. To the same church he wrote earlier, "God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty." Some readers think of a shepherd boy, fishermen, a carpenter's son: people nobody expected much from. Last, what it does not mean. It doesn't mean staying in harm, or calling cruelty a blessing, or pretending pain is pleasant. Paul's list is hardship for Christ's sake, not abuse to be endured in silence. The point is honesty: when you stop pretending to be strong, there's room for help, from God, in Paul's telling, and from people.

Name one place where you're not strong right now: patience that runs out, a fear, something you can't do, help you need. Say it plainly, without apologizing, and picture a clay jar in your hands, ordinary and a little chipped. If you pray, offer the weakness to God and ask for strength that isn't yours; if you don't, notice what it's like to stop pretending. If someone is harming you, or you're thinking of harming yourself, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Strength in weakness. Paul's discovery that when he stopped hiding his limits, a power not his own could rest on him: treasure in clay jars.
Your line: weak, then strong. The treasure was always in clay jars. See you tomorrow.

1391.title: Angry at God
1391.hook: the psalms, Job and Jeremiah all argue with God
1391.howItsDone: Some Christians pray the psalms of lament in services and alone, including their angry lines; some churches hold services of lament after tragedies, and pastors and spiritual directors encourage people to bring anger honestly to God in prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, strength in weakness: treasure in earthen vessels. Your line was weak, then strong.

A man sits with his feet locked in the stocks at a gate by the house of the LORD. He's been beaten for delivering God's message. The next morning he's let out. Later, the prophet Jeremiah turns to God: "O LORD, thou hast deceived me, and I was deceived: thou art stronger than I, and hast prevailed: I am in derision daily, every one mocketh me." You tricked me, he says, and look where it got me. It's still there, in the scriptures of church and synagogue alike.

Back in year one, David shouted at God in the Psalms. He has company. Psalm thirteen opens, "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever? how long wilt thou hide thy face from me?" Four times, how long. It's someone pounding on a door, and it was kept in the book God's people sang together. Then Job. Before God ever speaks, Job says, "I will not refrain my mouth; I will speak in the anguish of my spirit; I will complain in the bitterness of my soul." He keeps that promise. And he wants a hearing, not an exit: "Oh that I knew where I might find him! that I might come even to his seat! I would order my cause before him, and fill my mouth with arguments." He talks as if God's seat were a courtroom he's desperate to get into. Then what Jeremiah does next. After accusing God, he says he'll stop speaking God's name. And then: "But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay." Angry, and unable to walk away. Anger at God, in these texts, can be a sign of how close the relationship still is. Some readers put it this way: you don't shout at someone you've stopped believing in. Some Christians were taught that anger at God is a sin to be hidden. These texts show another way: bring it, honestly, to the one it's aimed at. In the Psalms, that is prayer.
screen: `JOB: I WILL NOT REFRAIN MY MOUTH.`
`A FIRE SHUT UP IN MY BONES.`
`BRING IT TO THE ONE IT'S AIMED AT.`

segments.voice: Let one anger come up that you haven't said out loud: an unfairness, a loss, a prayer that went nowhere, something done to you or someone you love. If you pray, tell God plainly, in your own words or the psalm's, how long; if you don't, say it to the empty room or on paper. If the anger ever turns toward harming yourself or someone else, call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
Angry at God. The honest fury of Jeremiah, Job and the Psalms, kept in scripture as a kind of prayer.
Your line: he can take it. Jeremiah was furious, and stayed. Rest well.

1392.title: Faith and reason
1392.hook: Christians have long held both are gifts from the same God
1392.howItsDone: Christians bring faith and reason together in Bible study groups, catechism classes, theology and apologetics; Catholic teaching in particular has written at length on how the two work together, and Protestant and Orthodox churches each have their own traditions of careful thinking about faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the psalms, Job and Jeremiah argue with God out loud. Your line was he can take it.

A Bible study, a Tuesday night, folding chairs in a circle. A teenager in the back raises her hand and asks what others have been sitting on: if I keep asking questions, does that mean I don't have enough faith? It's an old worry, that thinking hard is the opposite of believing, that the mind is a door you close before you kneel. A line of Christian thinkers answers that worry with a no. Faith and reason, they say, come from the same God, and he isn't afraid of either one.

Asked for the great commandment, Jesus answers: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind." The mind is on the list. Thinking is one of the ways love is given. Then Isaiah, where God opens what sounds like a case at law: "Come now, and let us reason together, saith the LORD." An invitation to talk it through. In Acts, Paul preaches in a town called Berea, and the people there "received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so." They checked the apostle against the scrolls, and the text calls them more noble for it. A letter of Peter asks Christians to "be ready always to give an answer to every man that asketh you a reason of the hope that is in you with meekness and fear." A reason, and a gentle one. Anselm of Canterbury described his work as faith seeking understanding: faith goes first, then goes looking. Pope John Paul II began a letter on this subject with a picture: faith and reason are like two wings, and the human spirit rises on both toward the truth. Christians weigh the two wings differently. Some put trust in how far reason can reach toward God on its own. Others stress how easily a human mind wanders, and lean harder on what God reveals. But in these texts, nobody is asked to switch the mind off. A bird with one wing doesn't get far.

Pick one thing you hold to be true: that people are mostly good, that prayer matters, that there's nothing after death. Ask it three plain questions: where did I first get this, why do I still hold it, and what would I say if a friend asked why? You don't have to change it; look at it in good light, the way the Bereans unrolled the scrolls, and if you pray, ask for an honest mind.
Faith and reason. Trust and careful thinking, gifts of the same God, these thinkers say, meant to fly together.
Your line: two wings. The Bereans were called noble for checking the scrolls. Go gently.

1393.title: Miracles
1393.hook: Christians differ on how often God acts beyond nature; all see the world itself as a gift
1393.howItsDone: Christians differ on miracles today: Pentecostal and charismatic churches pray openly for healings and wonders, the Catholic Church investigates reported miracles (including in naming saints), and some Protestant traditions emphasize God's work through ordinary means.

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith and reason: the mind on the list, and the Bereans checking the scrolls. Your line was two wings.

"This beginning of miracles did Jesus in Cana of Galilee." That's how John sums up a wedding. The wine ran out. Jesus told the servants to fill six stone waterpots with water, and they filled them to the brim. What was carried to the steward of the feast was wine, and the steward said the good wine had been kept until now. A strange first wonder: no fever cured, no storm stilled, just a party that didn't have to end early. And it opens a question Christians still talk through: how often does God act beyond the ordinary run of things?

You met this wedding in year one. Where the King James says miracles, John's Greek says signs. A sign points somewhere. At Cana, John says, Jesus "manifested forth his glory; and his disciples believed on him." The wine pointed at the one who made it. Then the honest disagreement. Christians differ on how often God acts beyond nature today. In Pentecostal and charismatic churches, people pray boldly for healings and wonders now, and tell of seeing them. The Catholic Church investigates reported miracles carefully, including when it names saints. Some Protestants hold that the dramatic sign gifts belonged mainly to the age of the apostles, and that God now works chiefly through ordinary means: scripture, prayer, people, medicine. Each is a Christian answer, held with conviction. Underneath them all runs a thread. Augustine, preaching on this same wedding, pointed at the vineyards. The God who turned water into wine at Cana, he said, does it every year, slowly, through rain and root and vine, and people stop marveling only because it happens every season. The Psalms sound close: "The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork." And in Psalm 139: "I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made." The sky as a sign. Your own body as a sign. Whatever a Christian believes about Cana-style wonders today, these texts keep pointing at the ordinary world and calling it marvelous. Rain turning into grapes. A heart that keeps beating while you sleep.

Pick one ordinary thing within reach, your own hand, a glass of water, the light on the wall, and look at it as if nobody had ever shown it to you. Where did it come from, and what had to go right for it to be here? Stay with it until it starts to feel a little strange, and if you pray, say a plain thank you for it.
Miracles. Signs, in John's word: wonders that point past themselves. And for Augustine, the slow wonders of every season too.
Your line: every day a miracle. A week that began in the dark night ends on wonder. Rest well.

chat.says: Do Christians think miracles still happen today, or was that just back then?
options: They differ: some pray for wonders today; others say God works mostly through ordinary means.
John calls them proofs, so a Christian only believes after seeing one firsthand.
Augustine said Cana was a one-off, and that ordinary vines are no wonder at all.
chat.meaning: Christians differ on how often God acts beyond nature today. And Augustine pointed at the vineyards: water into wine, slowly, every year.
